discovery: Quantum key distribution: founding quantum cryptography based on the uncertainty principle and entanglement

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, USA

nominees.name: Artur K. Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) showed that the quantum no-cloning principle and measurement disturbance permit key distribution whose security rests on the laws of physics rather than computational assumptions. Ekert (1991) independently showed that entanglement and violation of Bell inequalities can certify secrecy, linking the foundations of quantum mechanics directly to a practical task and seeding device-independent security. These ideas turned Bell-test physics into an experimental frontier: fibre QKD networks spanning thousands of kilometres, measurement-device-independent protocols, and satellite-to-ground entanglement-based key distribution over 1,200 km. Quantum cryptography was the first quantum technology to reach real-world deployment and remains the conceptual template for the quantum internet. The 2022 prize honoured entanglement experiments; the 2025 prize honoured macroscopic quantum circuits. Recognising the inventors of quantum key distribution would complete the recognition of the second quantum revolution's founding ideas.
